name: Old-growth folk
one_line: They never cleared the forest; they cut it to the stump and it kept giving: coppice poles, a mound of charcoal smoking in the glade, and a garden of maize, beans and squash under the old trees.

needs: hazel, ash, maple or alder to cut to the stump
a deep-soiled flat for one garden-sized clearing, and a stream or spring

staples: maize, beans and squash from the clearing
hazelnuts, beech mast, acorns and chestnuts in autumn
deer and small game from the coppice edge; honey from wild hives
how: the Three Sisters plot in a small clearing
nutting in autumn, the woods' own harvest
snares and the spear along the cut stands, where the browse is
smoking a hollow tree for its comb
preserve: corn braided by the husk and hung under the roof
meat smoked over a slow fire; honey keeps itself

fuel.note: coppice poles are the fuel crop: hazel and ash cut to the stump and back in seven years; branch and brush off the cut for kindling; oak and beech logs for the long night; the rainforest burns spruce and hemlock, resin-rich and always damp, so fatwood and pitch matter more there

shelter.form: a longhouse of bent poles and bark sheets, a row of hearths down the middle and several families under one roof; or pit-houses dug into a dry slope; a hurdle fence of hazel withies round the plot

TEMPERATE_DECIDUOUS.fuel: hazel and ash coppice; oak and beech logs for the night
TEMPERATE_DECIDUOUS.food: maize, beans and squash in the clearing; hazelnuts, acorns, beech mast; deer
TEMPERATE_DECIDUOUS.shelter: a bark longhouse on a pole frame; hazel hurdles round the plot
TEMPERATE_DECIDUOUS.palette: oak green, bark grey, hazel gold, charcoal black

TEMPERATE_RAINFOREST.fuel: vine maple coppice and redwood stump-sprouts; spruce and hemlock logs, fatwood from old stumps
TEMPERATE_RAINFOREST.food: the plot in the one sunny flat, squash and beans over maize; salal, huckleberry, bracken root; elk
TEMPERATE_RAINFOREST.shelter: poles and bark under the giants, moss-chinked; a pit-house in a dry terrace against the wet
TEMPERATE_RAINFOREST.palette: moss green, fog grey, redwood bark, black soil

knows: hazelnuts, beech mast and acorns (leached before eating)
wood sorrel, ramsons and fiddleheads in spring; elderberry and hawthorn at the edge
tinder fungus and punk wood off a dead birch or beech
plantkeeper.teaches_flavour: why the last-cut glade is where the bluebells and the butterflies are; why nettle and elder mark an old hearth
plantkeeper.teaches_practical: leach acorns in running water before you eat them; the death cap looks like supper and kills in a week; which fungus holds a coal

techniques.name: Coppicing
techniques.verb: cut hazel or ash to the stump in winter; it does not die, it throws up a crown of straight poles, ready again in about seven years
techniques.teaches: the first harmony technique, because it keeps the fire lit: a stool cut this way outlives any tree left alone, and a woodlot cut in rotation is a fuel crop with no clearing, the woods never emptier than one year's cut
techniques.unlocks: the player cuts a stool and comes back to poles; the camp's fuel ceiling without stripping its woods

techniques.name: The Three Sisters
techniques.verb: maize, beans and squash in one mound: the stalk holds the bean up, the bean feeds the soil, the squash leaf shades out the weeds
techniques.teaches: three plants that feed each other and then feed you; a clearing the size of a garden, never a field
techniques.unlocks: the forest's crop ceiling: corn braided under the roof, a pit of nuts, then the specialist

techniques.name: Charcoal burning
techniques.verb: stack the poles in a mound round a chimney, seal it with bracken and turf, light it and starve it of air for days, watching the smoke go from white to blue
techniques.teaches: nearly pure carbon, hotter than any wood; what the marsh smith's bloomery needs, so the two peoples are married by trade
techniques.unlocks: charcoal in the store; exchange with the marsh; the collier

techniques.name: Pitch and birch tar
techniques.verb: cook pine resin, or birch bark sealed in a pot with a second pot beneath to catch the tar, slow and without air
techniques.teaches: the oldest glue there is: Neanderthals hafted flint with birch tar fifty thousand years ago and more; glue for the spear, tar for the boat, pitch for the torch
techniques.unlocks: the maker glues and seals; resin torches

techniques.name: Resin torch
techniques.verb: dip a cattail head or a twist of bark in pine pitch
techniques.teaches: a brighter, longer flame that shrugs off drizzle

techniques.name: Fatwood
techniques.verb: split the resin-soaked heart out of an old pine stump; the tree left it there when it died
techniques.teaches: a torch found, not made; lights wet and burns hot

techniques.name: Ember carrier
techniques.verb: a live coal wrapped in tinder fungus or punk wood, then in bark
techniques.teaches: no light, but a coal for a day or more; the Iceman carried embers in a birch-bark box five thousand years ago. Fire is never made, only carried
techniques.unlocks: carry fire; lay a new hearth from it; it goes cold if neglected

techniques.name: Honey
techniques.verb: smoke the wild hive in the hollow tree and take part of the comb
techniques.teaches: the sweetest thing in the forest and the one food that never rots; take some and the bees stay
techniques.unlocks: honey in the store: a trade good

wants: an iron axe from the marsh smith

ladder: a fire under the old trees; the ember carried in
the clearing: maize, beans and squash in one plot
corn braided under the eaves, nuts in a bark-lined pit, smoke over the meat
the collier: the first one who does not gather
charcoal walks to the marsh smith; pots and salt walk back
growth.restraint: the coppice is the rule made wood: cut a different stand each winter, seven stands round the camp, and the woods are never emptier than one year's cut; the clearing stays a garden, not a field; the hive is smoked, never felled
growth.ceiling_hint: a deciduous forest with a deep-soiled flat reaches the village; the rainforest is rich in fuel and poor in maize and stays a few hearths

signatures.what: a flat black circle ten paces across where nothing grows, the soil studded with charcoal; the trees round its rim grow thin
signatures.restore: cleared: the collier burns on the old platform, and the circle is the size it always was
signatures.inherits: a level, stone-free pitstead; the first burn needs no clearing

signatures.what: many-trunked hazel and ash in ranks, a crown of thick stems out of one huge stool: the giveaway that someone cut here
signatures.restore: restored: cut back to the stump, the stools throw poles again next spring
signatures.inherits: the woodlot works from the first cut; stools older than any tree standing

signatures.what: a long rectangle of post-stubs with a row of hearth-stones down the middle, or round hollows dug into the slope
signatures.restore: restored: new poles in the old holes, the hearths relit in a row
signatures.inherits: level floors and a row of hearths

signatures.what: a small stone-lined pit with a black glazed rim and a broken pot in the bottom
signatures.restore: restored: a new pot set in the old pit

ruin.plants_differ: nothing on the charcoal platform, and the trees round it grow slow; the coppice stools wear a crown of stems from one root; nettle and elder on the old hearths and middens; the spring flowers thickest in the last-cut glade

aesthetic.silhouette: a long low roof under tall trees; a mound smoking in a clearing; ranks of straight poles against a rack; a hurdle fence round the plot
props: the tar pot in its pit

real_world.analogue: Coppice woodsmanship of lowland England (Bradfield Woods, Suffolk)
real_world.region: eastern England; the craft across temperate Europe
real_world.note: cut on rotation since at least 1252; some ash stools are thought to be over a thousand years old; hazel on a seven-year cycle for hurdles, chestnut and oak on longer ones; the woods Oliver Rackham wrote from

real_world.region: Europe and the Appalachians, into the 20th century
real_world.note: wood stacked round a chimney, sealed with bracken and turf, burned starved of air for days and watched day and night; about 30 kg of charcoal from 100 kg of wood, and the only fuel hot enough to work iron; the platforms are still flat black circles in the woods, with tree cover lower or absent
flint hafted with tar distilled from birch bark at Campitello (Italy, c. 200,000 years), Königsaue (Germany) and on a 50,000-year-old tool from the Dutch North Sea: the oldest glue we know

the Iceman carried tinder fungus (Fomes fomentarius) in his belt pouch and a birch-bark container blackened inside, with maple leaves and charcoal: embers wrapped to carry; his axe and arrows were hafted with birch tar

real_world.region: the Eastern Woodlands: present-day New York and Ontario
real_world.note: longhouses of bent poles and elm bark, about 24 m long, up to twenty families to a row of hearths; maize, beans and squash planted together in mounds, the women planting and the men clearing; corn braided from the rafters, food kept in bark-lined pits
the village wood between paddy and mountain, cut for firewood and charcoal every 15–20 years, its leaf litter carried to the fields; left uncut it closes to dark laurel forest and the butterflies go

real_world.region: the forests of central Europe, recorded from 959 CE
real_world.note: hives cut into old trees six metres up with a board over the door, smoked and part-emptied, the colony left to go on; honey hunting itself is older than any farming, painted on rock walls 8,000 years ago
